questions.q: State the theorem: "The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the ______ through the point of contact." Fill in the blank and draw a labelled diagram showing the right angle.
questions.a: Correct answer: "radius". The diagram must show a circle with centre O, point P on circumference, tangent line at P, radius OP, and a right angle symbol (⟂ or 90°) between OP and the tangent. A wrong answer like "diameter" or "chord" reveals the student confuses the specific segment from centre to point of contact with other line segments in the circle. A missing right angle symbol in the diagram shows the student recalls words but not the geometric relationship.

questions.q: In the figure, PT is a tangent to the circle with centre O at point P. If ∠OPT = 35°, what is wrong with this diagram? Explain why this situation is impossible using the theorem.
questions.a: The situation is impossible because the theorem states OP ⟂ PT, so ∠OPT must be exactly 90°. A given angle of 35° contradicts the fundamental property. If a student says "maybe the tangent is drawn incorrectly" or "the angle is measured from the other side", they misunderstand that the theorem is an absolute geometric truth — the radius to the point of contact is ALWAYS perpendicular to the tangent, no exceptions. The error reveals the student treats the theorem as a conditional rule rather than a universal property.

questions.q: A circle has centre O and radius 6 cm. From a point P on the circle, a tangent PT is drawn such that PT = 8 cm. Find the distance OT from the centre to the end of the tangent segment. Show all steps.
questions.a:
Given: OP = 6 cm (radius), PT = 8 cm (tangent segment), OP ⟂ PT (theorem).
Step 1: In right triangle OPT, right angle at P.
Step 2: By Pythagoras theorem, OT² = OP² + PT² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100.
Step 3: OT = √100 = 10 cm.
A wrong answer of 14 cm (adding 6+8) shows the student ignores the right angle and treats it as a straight line. An answer of 2 cm (subtracting 8-6) shows confusion about which side is the hypotenuse. The correct working must explicitly state "∠OPT = 90°" before applying Pythagoras.

questions.q: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O. The quadrilateral OAPB has ∠AOB = 110°. Find ∠APB. Explain why the sum of opposite angles in OAPB is 180°.
questions.a:
Since OA ⟂ PA and OB ⟂ PB (tangent-radius theorem), ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°.
In quadrilateral OAPB, sum of angles = 360°.
∠OAP + ∠OBP + ∠AOB + ∠APB = 360°
90° + 90° + 110° + ∠APB = 360°
∠APB = 360° - 290° = 70°.
The opposite angles ∠AOB (110°) and ∠APB (70°) sum to 180° because the other two angles are both 90° (sum = 180°). A student who answers 110° (same as ∠AOB) or 250° (360°-110°) fails to use the two right angles from the tangent-radius property. This tests whether the student can combine the theorem with quadrilateral angle sum — a classic board exam pattern.

questions.q:
A student solves: "In the figure, PT is a tangent at P, OP = 5 cm, OT = 13 cm. Find PT." Their working:
OT² = OP² + PT² (Pythagoras)
13² = 5² + PT²
169 = 25 + PT²
PT² = 144
PT = 12 cm
Is this solution fully correct? If not, identify the missing step that would lose a mark in the board exam.
questions.a: The calculation is numerically correct but the solution is INCOMPLETE for board exam marking. The student must explicitly state: "Since PT is a tangent at P and OP is the radius, OP ⟂ PT (tangent is perpendicular to radius at point of contact). Therefore ∠OPT = 90° and triangle OPT is a right triangle." Without this justification, the application of Pythagoras theorem is not grounded in the theorem. In CBSE marking, 1 mark is typically allocated for stating the perpendicular property and identifying the right angle. The missing step is the geometric reasoning, not the arithmetic.

questions.q: Create a real-world problem involving a circular water tank of radius 3.5 m where a straight pipe touches the tank at exactly one point. The pipe makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal ground. Find the length of the pipe from the point of contact to where it meets the ground, given the tank's centre is 2 m above ground level. Draw the diagram and identify where the tangent-radius perpendicularity is used.
questions.a: A good answer constructs: Circle (tank) centre O, 2 m above ground. Radius OP = 3.5 m to point of contact P. Tangent line (pipe) at P meets ground at T. OT is not vertical — the pipe is at 30° to horizontal. The right angle ∠OPT = 90° is the key. Drop perpendicular from O to ground at M (OM = 2 m). The geometry requires coordinate geometry or trigonometry: OP = 3.5, ∠OPT = 90°, ∠PT(ground) = 30°. Student must use the perpendicular property to set up the right triangle, then apply trigonometry. A poor answer ignores the 90° at P and tries to use the 30° directly with the radius, showing they don't recognise the right triangle formed by radius and tangent.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The tangent to a circle at any point P is ______ to the radius OP drawn to the point of contact P.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a bicycle wheel ______ the ground at exactly one point — the tyre is the circle, the ground is the tangent line, and the spoke from the centre to the ground contact point is the radius.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can state the theorem precisely using correct geometric notation (OP ⟂ tangent at P), identify the right angle in any diagram involving a tangent and radius, apply the perpendicular property to find unknown angles or lengths using Pythagoras theorem, and use this property as a step in multi-part geometry problems involving.
